chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
title: Dress: George E. Lee's band to sweatshirts and the MJQ
summary: He says he became a musician partly for the dignity of dress and regrets the sloppiness of the Birdland era.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: That's part of it, yes. Another part is when you come to work in sweatshirts. Because one of the reasons I started playing music was because I told you I admired the way George E. Lee's band...
They had coal black, charcoal, oxford, what do you call it, black, oxford gray.
They had oxford gray coats. Nice cut. They had pearl gray vests and black and white tie and gambler stripe pants and patent
leather shoes. Now they looked so pretty that, you see, in those days all musicians were invited to the best of homes when they'd go on a trip.

Like they were invited to doctors homes, lawyers. Because that's the way they were raised. I mean, you carried yourselves right and you dressed very well. And that's one of the reasons that I wanted to play. And Herschel used to always look so, he was a typical, one of the kinds of musicians I was telling you about. Always with a pretty collar and tie and everything.
So that's one of the reasons I wanted to be a musician. When it got to Birdland stage, they'd come to work in anything. Sneakers, sweatshirt, it's getting a little better now I think.
Do you think it's turned again?

I think it's getting better. At least they are wearing, they are not as sloppy-looking. The musicians, I don't mean the rock and rollers because I don't know what the hell they wear. They can wear anything. Old floppy hats. But I notice musicians are beginning to dress a little bit more than they did in Birdland.
Well I guess that there will be like a pendulum swing sort of thing.
Well of course, then there was, there was the example of the Modern Jazz Quartet which seem to go to another extreme in that period. I mean, they looked like Undertakers. (LAUGHTER).
That's what we used to call them. The Four Undertakers. (LAUGHTER). That's exactly what they looked like. Four undertakers. They played well though.
